summary: Screw-pile light at the mouth of the Patapsco River, lit in 1856; automated in 1948, moved to Baltimore's Inner Harbor in 1988 and now a museum.

structures.note: First house. LighthouseFriends describes a round iron dwelling forty feet across; the Register describes square cast-iron panels (and elsewhere a wooden square house). Replaced later in the 19th century.

Present round house of riveted rolled-iron plates, two stories and a lantern, built about the last quarter of the 19th century (Register); date of replacement not determined. Moved to Pier 5, Baltimore, in 1988.

access.note: On Pier 5 at Baltimore's Inner Harbor. Museum hours (checked 2026-10-27): open Friday to Sunday, 10 am to 5 pm, Memorial Day to Labor Day; closed the rest of the year.

facts.agency: City of Baltimore (owner); Historic Ships in Baltimore (museum)

events.note: Tower established and keeper's quarters 1855 per the archive; LighthouseFriends says the work was completed in 1855. The Register gives 1856.
Light first exhibited 10 January 1856
Ice floes in January 1884 broke an iron pile (LighthouseFriends); the Register says ice that year destroyed one screw pile
Fifteen clusters of wooden piles driven round the light as ice breakers
Riprap placed round the base: about 790 cubic yards (Board report) or 700 (Register)
About 300 tons of riprap placed round the light against ice
Keeper C. W. Evans rescued six men from a disabled launch on 8 July
Schooner Catherine icebound off the station in January; the tender Maple towed her to Baltimore Light Station
Assistant keeper G. C. Hunley and additional keeper W. M. Goesky helped rescue two women and one man from a disabled motor boat on 7 August
Tug Point Breeze sank off Seven-Foot Knoll on 21 August
Keeper Thomas J. Steinhise pulled five men from the water; one more man found dead
Thomas J. Steinhise awarded a silver lifesaving medal
Coast Guard automated the light
Coast Guard declared the house excess property
Mariners' Museum, Newport News, gave up its claim to the house
Archive: discontinued 1987
Title passed from the Coast Guard to the City of Baltimore (Register; LighthouseFriends dates the transfer of the house to the city's move in October 1988)
Moved from the Knoll to Pier 5, Inner Harbor, October 1988; cost $600,000 (LighthouseFriends)
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, 22 August 1989
Became part of the Baltimore Maritime Museum

corrections.why: The archive records the light at 43 feet (about 13.1 m) above mean high water, and LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane of 44 feet (about 13.4 m). Neither source supports 17.0 m. The 17.0 m figure may come from another source or describe a later light; a human should check.
LighthouseFriends describes the historic light as a fixed white light. The recorded Fl WR 6s may describe the modern light on the site; the page should say which light it means.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive and LighthouseFriends date the tower to 1855 (established, completed); the Register gives 1856 as the year it was built and went into operation. LighthouseFriends gives 10 January 1856 as the first exhibition of the light, which is the date the story uses for first light.

notes_for_editor: Keepers: the 173 roster lines are the archive's own lines (person slugs attached because each line is the archive record's stint); the count of 29 head, 107 first and 37 second assistants is ours. J. W. Frazier (-1936) has no start year in the archive. Not checked against the NARA registers. Disagreements left open in the story: (1) first house round iron (LighthouseFriends) vs square cast-iron panels and a wooden square house (Register); (2) 1850 and $10,000 (Register) vs 1851 and $17,000 (LighthouseFriends); (3) Bodkin Point (Register) vs Bodkin Island (LighthouseFriends); (4) earlier rejected design: 60-foot brick tower (Register) vs Lewis's wood-and-iron plan (LighthouseFriends); (5) riprap 1894: 790 cubic yards (Board) vs 700 (Register); (6) first light 1855/1856. Year of the 1894 riprap: the Board report is for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1894, but its entry mentions an October 1894 job and then 'in November'; the story reads November 1894 as following that October, and LighthouseFriends dates it 1894. Worthington: the archive lists Joseph F. Worthington as head keeper for 1870 and as first assistant 1874-75; his own February 1870 letter (as quoted by the museum) calls him an assistant keeper. Not resolved. Hunley: archive first assistant 1927-31; Bulletin 1928 calls him assistant keeper; consistent. Goesky: named by the Bulletin as additional keeper, not on the archive roster; added as an 'other' row. C. W. Evans (Bulletin 1922, keeper) and Caleb W. Evans (archive first assistant 1921-22): not linked; the sources do not say they are one man. Steinhise rescue: the Bulletin says five pulled into the boat and one more found dead; LighthouseFriends says six pulled aboard, one dead (consistent). The AP report of 21 Aug 1933 names chief engineer Percy Harrison as lost with his body ashore at the lighthouse; the sources do not connect him to the dead man, and the story says so. LighthouseFriends' wave and wind figures are its own; no other source read gives them. Ownership: the Register says title passed in 1988; the archive records discontinuance in 1987. The LighthouseFriends move date (October 1988) is used. Only one source each for: the 1884 tender Holly and the removal of the keepers (LighthouseFriends); the 1948 McCabe quote (LighthouseFriends, from the Baltimore Sun, not read); the 1969-1975 Mariners' Museum episode (LighthouseFriends); the 1982 inspection (LighthouseFriends). Museum-quoted material (1870 letter, 1880 rule, 1913-16 inspection, January 1936 district report, Eva Bowling's 1936 interview) is cited to the Historic Ships page as quoted there; the originals were not read. Position: the record's coordinates are the Pier 5 museum site (OpenStreetMap). The archive gives the original station in the bay at 39 09.17 N, 76 24.35 W; the editor may want both shown. Structures: the record's 'tower, built 1855, 16.0 m, standing' has no height source among those read. Record's Rowlett (tower 2, built 1987; first lit 1856) not verified: the Rowlett Maryland page read did not reach this station. Hours: taken from the museum's hours page and the lighthouse page, both read 2026-10-27; seasonal hours may change. The lighthouse page showed it closed that day. OCR: the Evening Star and Washington Daily News quotes are from OCR text; check the page images before quoting 'Percy Harrison, 55'. The 1884 German passage is translated by us (sources 15); the English in the story is ours. The Heap (1889) page is cited as scan p. 121 (printed page not confirmed). The Johnson (1889) page is p. 27 by the corpus index. Wikipedia not used. The lens's present location is unknown; the archive lists no current optic. Photos: none sourced; LighthouseFriends and the museum have photos under their own copyright. Fact-check 2026-10-27 (independent pass): quote check found all 114 quotes in their sources on the first run. Changed: the lede now names the station and no longer calls the first house 'iron' (the Register describes it three ways); the 'new kind of foundation' sentence was removed (no footnote gave it); the age '55' was removed from Percy Harrison (the Evening Star text is OCR and the page image is not reachable through the research tools, so the age was not confirmed); 'the museum that runs the pier' was rewritten to what LighthouseFriends and Historic Ships say (the link between the two names rests on the shared telephone number); 'the original station in the bay' was replaced with the archive's own coordinates and location text; the 173-entry keeper count is now marked as our count by role; Worthington's letter is now reported as a resignation, and the archive's principal-keeper listing for 1870 is stated as a disagreement; 'makeshift' was removed (not in the cited page); the 1894 diver finding now says 'all the water braces'; the riprap is 'laid around the site' (the Board's report says 'distributed about the site'); metres added to feet. Checked against sources: the NRHP text, LighthouseFriends, the USLHS roster (173 lines: 29 principal, 107 first, 37 second assistants, ending 1945), the Board reports (pages 96-97, 99, scan 54 for Johnson), the Bulletins by PDF page, the Evening Star and Washington Daily News pages, the German passage, and the Historic Ships pages. Goesky: the Bulletin body OCR reads 'Goeshy', but the 1928 Bulletin index reads 'Goesky', so the spelling stands; not confirmed on the page image. Johnson is cited by scan page 54 because the printed page is not in the OCR text.
